k-1.x_notes: Same six problems as Y, with nearly identical actual-size boards: blue-only covering with impossible cases (odd area and an 8-triangle trapezoid with 5 up and 3 down), fewest greens on triangles of side 2-4 (answers 2,3,4), fewest blocks, a rhombus-placing game whose strips and hexagon give a good mix of first and second player wins, and find-all tilings. Strength: the find-all problems give extra boards (3 boards for 2 tilings, 4 for 3, 8 for 6), so the page does not give away how many tilings there are. Weaknesses: P6 has children draw each of the 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon on half-inch drawing hexagons, which is a hard fine-motor task for kindergartners and less concrete. The game answers are the words 'first/second', which pre-readers cannot read. There is no rule that says to use only the small blocks, although upscale blocks are on the table. With extra boards and no adult notes, a parent volunteer has no way to tell children that they are done.
k-1.y_notes: Essentially the same packet, and the math is equally correct. Strengths: P6 is fully concrete, with six actual-size boards on which children build and compare all 6 tilings side by side, so nothing has to be drawn at small scale. The game uses large '1 2' numerals, and the wording 'first player can always win' is clearer. The shared rules add 'use only the small blocks'. Weakness: in P3 (2 and 3 boards) and P6 (6 boards) the number of boards equals the number of tilings, which takes away the question of whether all of them have been found. P6 also needs many blue blocks (8 per board).
k-1.reason: The packets are nearly identical. Y keeps the hardest find-all problem physical at actual size and makes the game readable for pre-readers, which matters more for K-1 than X's advantage of not revealing the solution counts.

grades-2-3.x_notes: The content is strong and correct. It has good possible/impossible boards: the star tiles, the side-3 triangle and the 7-up/5-down trapezoid do not, the hourglass is balanced overall but each half is unbalanced, and of the two side-2 hexagons with holes, the one with two up-holes fails and the one with mixed holes tiles. Fewest greens on triangles of side 2-5, generalized to side 10 and side 100. The chevron comparison is sound: chevrons can never beat blues and actually do worse on small triangles. Inventing a 20-triangle board that needs 6 greens is achievable (13 up, 7 down). P7 has a clean rule (I checked that every placement of one up and one down green works on the side-2 hexagon). Weaknesses: the side-5 triangle on page 4 has no label, and P3's text does not say it continues on the next page. P4 asks only for numbers, not for a reason. There is no small-blocks rule.
grades-2-3.y_notes: The same boards and problems, with identical diagrams. It adds 'on this page and the next' to P3, so the unlabeled page-4 triangle is clearly part of P3. P4 asks children to explain why nobody can use fewer, and gives more lines for it. The shared rules say 'use only the small blocks'. P7 asks children to explain why the other places can never work, which is the coloring argument and the right proof target for this age. There are no new defects.
grades-2-3.reason: The packets are virtually identical. Y makes small but useful clarity fixes (the P3 page continuation, the small-block rule, a justification prompt in P4) and introduces no new problems.

grades-4-5.x_notes: The sequence is strong and correct. It covers the 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon, the flip graph, flip distances on the 2-2-2 hexagon (I decoded the pictured tilings: A to B is 3 flips, C to D is 4, and E to F is 8, the diameter), parity of closed flip walks, ribbons, the full count of 20, and a 1-3-3 hexagon capstone (20 tilings, C(6,3)). The P3 pictures are clean. Weaknesses: P4 says 'start with any covering ... from Problem 3', but from E or F (the two cube-corner tilings, each with only one available flip) no 4-flip return without repeating a hexagon exists. F is the covering already on the board after P3, so children are likely to start there and get stuck. P4 also has only two lines and no boards to record the cycle. P2 makes children redraw all six coverings from P1 before connecting them, which is copying busywork.
grades-4-5.y_notes: The same mathematics and boards. P4 fixes the start at covering A, which does have a valid 4-flip cycle, and gives five small hexagons to record it. In P2, children number their coverings and draw the flip graph on the numbers, so they do not redraw everything. P6 is worded clearly: 'on the hexagon board', and it asks children to find and justify the smallest E-to-F number. P7 allows children to draw or list the tilings, which invites ribbon notation. The rules include 'use only the small blocks'. Weaknesses: the P3 covering pictures keep faint grid lines inside each rhombus, which makes them busier to read. P4's page is mostly empty space.
grades-4-5.reason: In X, P4 sets a real trap: children who start from the covering they just finished (F) or from E are asked to do something impossible. Y specifies a working start, gives recording space, and removes the redraw busywork in P2, which outweighs X's slightly cleaner P3 pictures.

overall.reason: The two packets share nearly all their mathematics and diagrams, and both are mathematically sound. Every substantive difference favors Y: the 4-5 starting covering in P4 is fixed (X's 'any covering' includes cases where the task is impossible), the 2-3 page flow is clearer, the K-1 find-all work is kept physical, and the shared rules say to use only the small blocks. X's only real advantages are that its find-all boards do not reveal the counts and that its covering pictures are slightly cleaner.
